ctx.x: Let’s suppose you went to a party and someone asks you what you do and, “Well I play a lot of Latin jazz.” And that person said, “What makes Latin jazz different from jazz?”

Okay. We have jazz the way we know it, the swing stuff, the bebop, which I wanted to be a jazz drummer at first before I ever got into the Latin thing. So in college I was into Mel Lewis, you know, Buddy Rich of course, Stan Kenton. I went to North Texas State University. So I was studying and playing in the lab. I’ve always loved straight ahead jazz you know and of course I used to listen to all the bebop stuff, Miles Davis and all that stuff. But then one day somebody in the dorm heard me playing some Mexican…

blew my mind away because of the rhythm. It was so strong. And then I started to hear like the bands of Machito, who did a lot of what we call now Latin jazz for me it’s the marriage of both because for instance in straight ahead Latino, like a dance tune, it might have one chord like we did yesterday. It might have a 1-4-5 progression [scats] or a 2-5- 1 or a 1-6-2-5. You know, the basic chord structure, and of course jazz — it still has that but it might have so many other chords, especially like a ballad. So…
